The human plateau began to shift. The posts spread through the feeds like wildfire: it was prime time, just before the end of the workday. The viewer count instantly jumped from two hundred thousand to two hundred and fifty. Online-media bots picked up the story and began churning out news about the provocative stream by "the most innovative business coach of our generation." And a woman, no less!

Now three hundred and fifty thousand people from all over the world were watching, liking, sharing, and paying real dollars to ask Freya a question. Three hundred and sixty. Three hundred and seventy. Every new thousand took Freya's breath away. And then it was time to answer.

The main thing was not to let this chat with her followers turn into a group date on Tinder.

*"Do you have kids?"* a stranger asked. *"How do you succeed when you've got four of them?"*

Freya wanted to answer: *"You don't."* But, first of all, moms on maternity leave made up forty-eight percent of her audience, so it was a sore subject. And second, you couldn't answer a follower like that when she had most likely scraped together those fifty bucks out of the money she should have been giving her kids for lunch. So Freya fell back on a polite, pre-rehearsed answer.

"Everyone defines success for themselves," she said. "If you've always dreamed of being a mom or a dad, then your children *are* your capital. The key is to stick to your investment strategy and not hand your capital over to unvetted funds."

*"Are you married?"* someone asked, having donated the minimum five dollars.

Questions like that Freya now simply left unanswered. Fortunately, the stream of more interesting (and more expensive!) questions flushed all the cheap provocations down the toilet.

Besides, her joke had landed. The chat was thrilled, and the viewer count kept climbing: a clip of her answer had already gone viral on Twitter. But fame brings responsibility, and the questions veered sharply into Tinder group-date territory.
